title: Devanagari
hook: one question: does a holy text open on your own?
tomorrow: Priya copies half of Nani's line. which of the week's marks are in it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Devanagari's conjuncts: two letters holding on when no vowel comes between, and abhyasa, coming back. Today, one question.
screen: `A KNOT IS TWO LETTERS HOLDING ON.`

segments.voice: So much can be learned alone now: a video for fixing a sink, an app for chords, a course at two in the morning. Learning the letters can go that way too. But the letters are a door into texts people have lived by for a long time. So here's the question: once you can read a holy text, can you read it on your own?
screen: `A VIDEO FOR EVERYTHING.` → `THE LETTERS ARE A DOOR.` → `CAN YOU READ IT ALONE?`

segments.voice: The Taittiriya Upanishad answers with a rhythm. One passage lists what a good life holds: right conduct, truth, discipline, calm, welcoming guests. And after every single one, the same refrain: and study and teaching. Svadhyaya and pravachana. Reading for yourself, and receiving it from someone and handing it on, always together. When students finish, the teacher's parting words include: don't neglect study and teaching. And in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna to learn by bowing, by asking, by serving; those who have seen the truth will teach you. So the tradition's answer: read it yourself, yes, and also with someone who has lived inside it. A neighbor says something close. In the book of Acts, a traveler from Ethiopia is riding home, reading the prophet Isaiah aloud in his chariot. Philip runs alongside and asks: "Understandest thou what thou readest?" The traveler answers: "How can I, except some man should guide me?" And he invites Philip up to sit beside him. Shared: two traditions that say a holy text opens best with a guide. And an honest difference. In Acts, Philip reads Isaiah as pointing to Jesus, and the story ends with the traveler baptized. In the Gita, the guide is a teacher who has seen the truth, and the learning goes on through asking and serving.
screen: `AND STUDY AND TEACHING.` · `ASK, SERVE, LEARN FROM ONE WHO HAS SEEN.` · `ACTS: HOW CAN I, EXCEPT SOME MAN GUIDE ME?` · `SHARED: A GUIDE BESIDE YOU.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes close and bring to mind one person who once explained something so it finally made sense. See their face, their hands, the place you were sitting. Stay there with them quietly; if you pray, you can give thanks for them in your own words.
Devanagari: letters you can learn alone, opening texts the tradition says to read with a guide.
Your line: Devanagari. Read it yourself, and read it with someone who has lived inside it. Back tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Hindus first learn a text like the Gita with a teacher or an elder, verse by verse, often in a class or a study group, alongside reading it on their own.

chat.meaning: The Taittiriya pairs study with teaching, and the Gita says learn from one who has seen. Reading alone is fine; a guide opens more.

Taittiriya Upanishad.meaning: an Upanishad that pairs every virtue with study and teaching

svadhyaya.meaning: one's own study of a sacred text

pravachana.meaning: teaching: receiving a text and handing it on

Arjuna.meaning: the warrior Krishna teaches in the Gita

Philip.meaning: an early follower of Jesus in the book of Acts

sources.quoted: How can I, except some man should guide me?

notes: Unity thread (wisdom day): shared with Christianity, in its own words (Acts 8:30–31, KJV): a holy text opens best with a guide. Honest difference: in Acts, Philip 'preached unto him Jesus' (8:35) and the traveler is baptized (8:38); in the Gita (4.34) the guide is one who has seen the truth, approached by bowing, asking and serving. Neither ranked. 1427 used the Qur'an ('Read'), so this week's neighbor is different.

Taittiriya 1.9 lists ṛta, satya, tapas, dama, śama, the fires, guests and more, each followed by 'svādhyāya-pravacane ca'; 1.11.1 has 'svādhyāya-pravacanābhyāṃ na pramaditavyam'. The list in the voice is abridged and paraphrased. Confirm.

KJV 8:30 has 'Esaias' for Isaiah; the voice says Isaiah outside the quotation. 'Understandest thou what thou readest?' and 'How can I, except some man should guide me?' are exact KJV words; confirm punctuation.
